title: Lie–Kolchin triangular embedding for smooth connected solvable group schemes
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. All groups below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$; subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness are as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] and [def-weil-connected-scheme]. For $n\geq1$, let $B_n\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_n$ be the group of invertible upper triangular matrices and $U_n\subseteq B_n$ its subgroup of matrices with every diagonal entry equal to $1$. Thus their $A$-points, for a commutative $k$-algebra $A$, are the matrices just described. The general linear group is [def-sc-general-linear-group]. Assume that $k$ is algebraically closed [def-weil-algebraic-closure], and let $J$ be smooth, connected and solvable. Here solvable means having a finite descending series of closed subgroups, each normal in its predecessor, whose successive fppf group-sheaf quotients are commutative. There exist $n\geq1$ and a closed immersion of group schemes $J\hookrightarrow B_n$. A closed immersion is as in [def-weil-closed-immersion]. No characteristic-zero hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Theorem 16.30 (Lie–Kolchin), printed pp.334–335; Proposition 16.2(a)–(c), printed pp.324–325; faithful linear representations in Theorem 4.9. The solvability notion is the closed-subgroup normal-series notion of Chapter 6.

proof.text: Put $\Gamma=J(k)$. A solvable series $J=J_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq J_t=1$ gives subgroups $\Gamma_i=J_i(k)$. Since $J_i\to J_i/J_{i+1}$ has kernel $J_{i+1}$ and commutative target, $[\Gamma_i,\Gamma_i]\subseteq\Gamma_{i+1}$. Thus the abstract derived series $D^0\Gamma=\Gamma$, $D^{a+1}\Gamma=[D^a\Gamma,D^a\Gamma]$ satisfies $D^a\Gamma\subseteq\Gamma_a$ and terminates. We prove by induction on $s$ the stronger assertion: for every smooth connected affine finite-type $k$-group $H$ with $D^s(H(k))=1$, all nonzero simple rational representations have dimension one; hence every nonzero rational representation contains a stable line. Here simple means no nonzero proper group-scheme-stable subspace. The implication after the semicolon follows by taking a stable subspace of least positive dimension. Smoothness gives reducedness by [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced]; throughout, matrix equations holding at all $H(k)$ hold in $k[H]$ by [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing](2). In the base $s=0$, $H(k)=1$, so every matrix coefficient of $r-I$ is zero and every line is stable. This proves the base, including zero-dimensional $H$.

source.place: Theorem 16.30, pp.334–335; Proposition 6.30, p.132. Same derived-group proof with induction on the abstract derived length instead of dimension.

proof.text:
For the induction step let $s\geq1$, let $H$ satisfy the induction hypothesis at level $s$, and let $V
e0$ be a simple rational $H$-module. Take $N=D_H$ from [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup]. It is smooth, connected, normal, affine and finite type, and $N(k)=[H(k),H(k)]$. Hence $D^{s-1}(N(k))=1$. Apply the already proved induction assertion at $s-1$ to the restriction of $V$ to $N$: it has a stable line. The action on this line is a character $\chi:N	o\mathbf G_m$, so $V_\chi
e0$. By [lem-sfb-character-eigenspaces-independent], the set $S=\{\psi:V_\psi
e0\}$ is finite, and its eigenspaces are independent. All eigenspaces mean the all-algebras spaces defined in that node.

source.place: Theorem 16.30, p.334, through the finite set of characters; Corollary 6.19 and Proposition 6.20, pp.129–130.

proof.text: For $g\in H(k)$ and $n\in N(A)$, normality gives $r_A(n)r_A(g)(1\otimes v)=r_A(g)r_A(g^{-1}ng)(1\otimes v)=\chi_A(g^{-1}ng)r_A(g)(1\otimes v)$ for $v\in V_\chi$. Thus $gV_\chi=V_{\chi^g}$ with $\chi^g(n)=\chi(g^{-1}ng)$, and $H(k)$ permutes $S$. The stabilizer of $E=V_\chi$ therefore has finite index in $H(k)$. In a basis beginning with a basis of $E$, it is cut out on $H(k)$ by the lower-left matrix entries of $r(g)$, so it is the set of rational points of a closed subgroup $K\subseteq H$. Its finitely many distinct cosets are closed. They cover $|H|$: otherwise the open complement contains a nonempty principal affine open, whose nonzero finitely generated coordinate algebra has a maximal ideal and hence a $k$-point by [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing](1). Similarly, two such closed cosets cannot meet without a $k$-point in their intersection. They give a finite disjoint closed cover, hence a clopen partition. Connectedness forces just one coset. All lower-left entries vanish on $H(k)$ and therefore in $k[H]$ by reducedness and the vanishing principle. Consequently $E$ is $H$-stable as a group-scheme subspace. Simplicity gives $V=V_\chi$.

source.place: Theorem 16.30, pp.334–335, conjugation equation and closed finite-index stabilizer argument.

proof.text: Put $d=\dim V\geq1$. Every $n\in N(k)$ acts by $\chi(n)I_d$. By [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup], it is a finite product of commutators in $H(k)$. The determinant-homomorphism clause of [def-sc-general-linear-group] gives $\det(r([x,y]))=\det(r(x))\det(r(y))\det(r(x))^{-1}\det(r(y))^{-1}=1$, so $\chi(n)^d=1$. By smooth reducedness and [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing](2), the regular function $\chi^d-1$ on $N$ is zero. The underlying space of $N$ is consequently partitioned by the finitely many closed fibres $\chi^{-1}(a)$, where $a$ ranges over the distinct roots of $T^d-1$ in $k$. These fibres are disjoint and form a finite cover even when that polynomial has repeated roots: every prime of $k[N]$ contains one of its linear factors. Connectedness makes only one fibre nonempty; the identity lies over $1$, so every $n\in N(k)$ has $\chi(n)=1$. The vanishing principle again gives $\chi-1=0$ in $k[N]$. Thus $N$ acts trivially on $V$ over every algebra. No reducedness of $\mu_d$ is asserted or needed.

source.place: Theorem 16.30, p.335, determinant calculation and smooth-connected finite-image argument.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] the quotient $q:H\to Q=H/N$ represents the fppf sheaf quotient. Since $N$ acts trivially, $r$ descends: on any fppf local lift $h$ of $u\in Q(A)$ set $\bar r(u)=r(h)$; two lifts differ by $N$, so these values agree and glue in $\operatorname{GL}(V)$. This is a natural group homomorphism, hence a group-scheme morphism. The commutator morphism of $H$ factors through $N$ by [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup]. Local lifts of two points of $Q$ therefore commute modulo $N$, and the sheaf property makes $Q$ commutative. Apply [lem-sfb-commutative-group-representation-eigenline] to $\bar r$. Its stable line pulls back to an $H$-stable line, so simplicity of $V$ gives $d=1$. Together with the minimal-dimension argument of step 1, this completes the induction and gives a stable line in every nonzero rational representation of $J$.

source.place: Theorem 16.30, p.335, final descent to the commutative quotient and Corollary 16.14; fppf quotient interpretation: Section 5(j), pp.116–118.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-normal-subgroup-representation-kernel] to the trivial closed normal subgroup of $J$, obtaining $r:J\to\operatorname{GL}_n$, $n\geq1$, with trivial scheme-theoretic kernel. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] to write it as $J\to I\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_n$, with $J\to I$ identifying $I$ with the fppf quotient by that kernel. The quotient by the trivial subgroup is $J$ itself, so $J\simeq I$ and $r$ is a closed immersion. In particular this is a faithful rational representation on $k^n$, not just an injective map on $k$-points.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(b)⇒(c), p.325; Theorem 4.9 and Corollary 4.10, p.87. The existing prescribed-kernel and homomorphism nodes give the faithful representation.

proof.text: Construct a full $J$-stable flag in $V=k^n$ by induction on $\dim V$. For $V=0$ the empty flag suffices. For $V\ne0$, the assertion proved in steps 1–5 gives a stable line $L$. The action on $V/L$ is rational: in a basis starting with $L$, stability says the lower-left block is identically zero in $k[J]$, and the lower-right block defines the quotient action with invertible determinant. The induction on dimension gives a full stable flag in $V/L$; its inverse images, preceded by $0\subset L$, give a full stable flag in $V$. Choose successive basis vectors adapted to this flag. For every algebra $A$, preservation of each initial span says exactly that all entries below the diagonal vanish. Hence $r$ factors as a group homomorphism $f:J\to B_n\subseteq\operatorname{GL}_n$. On coordinate algebras the surjection $k[\operatorname{GL}_n]\to k[J]$ kills the below-diagonal variables, so the induced map $k[B_n]=k[\operatorname{GL}_n]/(x_{ij}:i>j)\to k[J]$ is surjective. This is precisely a closed immersion of affine schemes. Thus $f$ is the required closed immersion of group schemes with $n\geq1$.

source.place: Proposition 16.2(a)⇒(b)⇒(c), p.325; adapted-flag basis and quotient of coordinate algebras.
